evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: Sandy Shreve is a Canadian poet, editor and visual artist living on Pender Island, British Columbia.

evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: Shreve has written, edited and/or co-edited eight books and two chapbooks.

evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: Her latest poetry collection is "Waiting for the Albatross".

evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: Recent work has appeared in her chapbooks, "Cedar Cottage Suite" and "Level Crossing".

evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: Her work is widely anthologized and has won or been shortlisted for several awards, including the Earle Birney Prize (for "Elles", published in "Prism Magazine", 2000) and the Milton Acorn Peoples Poetry Award (for "Belonging", Sono Nis Press, 1997).

evidence.title: Sandy Shreve
evidence.text: She co-edited, with Kate Braid, the anthology "In Fine Form – The Canadian Book of Form Poetry" (2005) and "In Fine Form, 2nd edition - A Contemporary Look and Canadian Form Poetry"(2016); edited "Working For A Living", a collection of poems and stories by women about their work (Room of One’s Own, 1988) and founded BC’s "Poetry in Transit" program, which has been displaying BC poetry in SkyTrain cars and buses across the province since 1996.

evidence.title: The Poetry Collection
evidence.text: A University at Buffalo Libraries Special Collection, The Poetry Collection at the University at Buffalo, The State University of New York, is devoted to 20th century poetry in English and English translation.

evidence.title: The Poetry Collection
evidence.text: Founded by Charles David Abbott, the University at Buffalo's first Director of Libraries, The Poetry Collection contains over 100,000 volumes by every major and many minor poet writing in English.

evidence.title: The Poetry Collection
evidence.text: Recordings of poets reading from their own works, poets' notebooks, letters and manuscripts, and a wide variety of literary magazines are also included in this collection.

evidence.title: The Poetry Collection
evidence.text: Approximately 5,000 little magazine titles, 1,200 current subscriptions, and a number of portraits, sculptures, and photographs round out the collection.

evidence.title: The Poetry Collection
evidence.text: Also included in the Poetry Collection is the James Joyce Archive, the world's largest collection of James Joyce manuscripts, books and artifacts.

evidence.title: B. H. Fairchild
evidence.text: B.H. Fairchild (born 1942) is an American poet and former college professor.

evidence.title: B. H. Fairchild
evidence.text: His most recent book is "Usher" (W.W. Norton, 2009), and his poems have appeared in literary journals and magazines including "The New Yorker", "The Paris Review", "The Southern Review", "Poetry", "TriQuarterly", "The Hudson Review", "Salmagundi", "The Sewanee Review."

evidence.title: B. H. Fairchild
evidence.text: His third poetry collection, "The Art of the Lathe," winner of the 1997 Beatrice Hawley Award (Alice James Books, 1998), brought Fairchild's work to national prominence, garnering him a large number of awards and fellowships including the William Carlos Williams Award, Kingsley Tufts Poetry Award, California Book Award, Natalie Ornish Poetry Award, PEN Center USA West Poetry Award, National Book Award (finalist), Capricorn Poetry Award, and Rockefeller and Guggenheim fellowships.

evidence.title: B. H. Fairchild
evidence.text: The book ultimately gave him international prominence, as The Way Weiser Press in England published the U.K. edition of the book.

evidence.title: B. H. Fairchild
evidence.text: "The Los Angeles Times" wrote that ""The Art of the Lathe" by B.H. Fairchild has become a contemporary classic—a passionate example of the plain style, so finely crafted and perfectly pitched...workhorse narratives suffused with tenderness and elegiac music."

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: Kevin MacNeil is a Scottish novelist, poet and playwright born and raised in the Outer Hebrides.

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: His latest novel, "The Brilliant & Forever", was published by Polygon in March 2016.

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: MacNeil's previous novels, "A Method Actor's Guide to Jekyll and Hyde" (Polygon, 2011) and best-selling debut, "The Stornoway Way" (Hamish Hamilton, 2005), were both published to widespread critical acclaim.

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: MacNeil’s first book, the poetry collection "Love and Zen in the Outer Hebrides" (Canongate, 1998), won the Tivoli Europa Giovani International Poetry Prize for best poetry collection published in Europe by a writer under 35.

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: He is also the author of "Be Wise Be Otherwise" (Canongate) and the plays "Sweetness", an adaptation of a novel by Swedish author Torgny Lindgren, and "The Callanish Stoned" (Theatre Hebrides), and his short stories have been published extensively.

evidence.title: Kevin MacNeil
evidence.text: MacNeil's anthology of poetry from the Scottish islands, "These Islands, We Sing", was published by Polygon in June 2011.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: Tales of Heichū (Heichū monogatari) belongs to the genre of uta monogatari poem tales that emerged in Japanese literature from the mid 10th to the early 11th centuries.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: As early as the "Collection of Ten-Thousand Leaves" ("Manyōshū"), a poetry collection completed around 759, there appeared poems introduced by brief prose narrations.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: The imperial court began to come alive with poetry from around this time.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: People exchanged poetry with one another on topics as diverse as love and politics and religion.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: Towards the end of the 9th century it was common for individual poets to keep compilations of their own verse, sometimes explaining in prose the circumstances behind a poem's composition.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: The highest honor was to have ones poem selected for inclusion in the "Collection of Ancient and Modern Poetry" (Kokinshū), the first imperial poetry collection, which was completed around 905.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: By the middle of the 10th century the idea of a poem paired with a prose narration seems to have taken hold, and "Tales of Ise" (Ise monogatari), "Tales of Heichū", and "Tales of Yamato" (Yamato monogatari) seem to have emerged at about this same time.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: Also, the second imperial poetry collection, "Collection of Later Poetry" (Gosenshū), commissioned in 951 and compiled shortly thereafter, has many narrative qualities.

evidence.title: Heichū Monogatari
evidence.text: The only extant manuscript of "Tales of Heichū" is a 61-page codex discovered in 1931 that seems to date from the Kamakura Period (1185–1333), some three hundred years after the work's probable date of composition.
